candidate.answerReason: The cut runs parallel to the fold halfway across the folded paper. Unfolding produces one rectangle with dimensions s by s/2 and two with dimensions s by s/4, giving a perimeter ratio of 5/6.

methods.label: Track the pieces after unfolding
methods.explanation:
Choose a length unit in which the original square has side \(4\). This is allowed because changing the unit multiplies both perimeters by the same amount and leaves their ratio unchanged.

Folding vertically in half makes a rectangle of height \(4\) and width \(2\). The cut shown runs vertically halfway across this folded rectangle, leaving two strips of width \(1\). The strip next to the fold unfolds into one rectangle of width \(2\). The other strip consists of two separate paper layers, giving two rectangles of width \(1\). All three pieces have height \(4\).

Each small rectangle therefore has perimeter \(2(4+1)=10\), while the large rectangle has perimeter \(2(4+2)=12\). The requested ratio is
\[
\frac{10}{12}=\boxed{\frac56},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Tracking one fold, halving lengths, and calculating rectangle perimeters are within elementary geometry and arithmetic.

candidate.annotationRationale: The targets are rectangle perimeters and their ratio. Rectangle and square properties, equal halves, and fraction reduction support the written method. The fold requires tracking which strip remains connected, but does not require the catalog's more advanced quadrilateral folding equations or ordered-stack procedures. No annotation establishes mastery.

review.mathematicalCheck: The depicted cut bisects the folded width parallel to the fold. For an original side of 4, the connected strip unfolds to a 4 by 2 rectangle, while the separate layers yield two 4 by 1 rectangles. Their perimeters are 12 and 10, so the requested ratio is 10/12=5/6. The explanation justifies both connectivity and the choice of units.
